topic: Family roles in consent with minors
stem: Sina, 15, a club soccer player, has been offered sessions on match nerves. Her father has signed the permission form. He says that in their family a new adult is met together, and that he expects to sit in. The consultant usually sees teenagers one-on-one. Talking with Sina at the side of the training field, the consultant asks what she makes of the plan. She shrugs: "My sister did this by herself at school, and she quit after one time. I'm the one who told Dad to come." How should the consultant set up the first sessions?
options: Meet with Sina, and send her father a summary she approves
Meet with her father first, and start with Sina once he is at ease
Meet with Sina and her father together, and review the setup later
Hold off on sessions, and leave the offer open to Sina
rationales: This is a sound arrangement for a teenager who wants private sessions and a parent who wants to be kept informed. Sina asked her father to come, so it would remove something she chose.
This suits a parent who is withholding permission until he understands the work. He has already signed the form and is ready to begin alongside her.

Her father's permission is in place, and Sina's assent turns out to be assent to sessions with him there. The consultant's usual format is a preference rather than a rule, and it can be revisited as the work goes on.
Waiting respects a minor who does not assent. Sina is not declining; she has arranged the condition under which she wants to come.
takeaway: With minors, permission and assent can point to a format other than the consultant's usual one.

stem: A consultant new to the fire service has spent six weeks riding along with a city department's crews. At first they called her "the campus doctor." Now a senior captain saves her a seat at dinner, and engineers at two stations, separately, have asked how she would keep a clear head on the drive to a call. Last night the captain teased, "So do we get anything out of you, or do you just eat our chili?" What should she do next to build her credibility with the crews?
options: Teach a short skill at shift change
Ride along on more shifts
Survey the crews about their needs
Ask a captain to vouch for her work
rationales: She has been accepted, and crews at separate stations have named the same need. The captain's joke signals that presence has done its work; being useful is now what earns credibility in this setting.
Time on shift is how an outsider learns a tactical culture, and it has worked. The teasing suggests that more of it would start to look like having nothing to offer.
A survey helps when needs are unclear. Two stations have independently raised the same one, and a form would put off what they have asked for.
An insider's backing helps an outsider who is being kept at a distance. The captain already treats her as one of the crew, and nobody has yet seen any work to vouch for.
takeaway: Contextual intelligence includes noticing when a group has moved from sizing you up to expecting something of you.

stem: Valeria, a professional volleyball player in her second season at a club abroad, asks to see the club's consultant, who speaks only the local language. In a first talk she hunts for words but describes confidentiality and its limits back accurately. The consultant offers to arrange an interpreter. She laughs: "My agent, my doctor, my landlord: every time, somebody in the middle. This year I order my own coffee." Which arrangement for the sessions fits best?
options: Use a trained interpreter from outside the club
Use a trained interpreter by video from another city
Refer her to a consultant who speaks her first language
Speak directly in the local language
rationales: A trained, independent interpreter is the usual safeguard when a client wants one or cannot follow. Valeria follows well enough to consent, and her answer is about doing without a go-between.
Remote interpreting protects privacy where every local interpreter is known to the client. Nobody's identity is her concern; she does not want a third person at all.
Work in a first language can be best when feelings cannot be put into words otherwise. She wants to use the new language and has sought out this consultant.
She can give informed consent in the language, and her remark tells the consultant that managing without a go-between matters to her. Checking meaning protects accuracy while respecting that choice.
takeaway: When understanding is adequate, language arrangements follow the client's wishes rather than the provider's default.

stem: A consultant is assessing pre-competition anxiety in a national goalball squad. The players, who have visual impairments ranging from partial sight to no light perception, variously use large print, braille, or neither. All of them text and email from their own phones throughout the day. After a federation survey last year, one told the consultant, "Sighted teams fill theirs in and nobody hears a thing. We got to say ours out loud to a staff member." Others agreed. Which way of gathering the players' ratings fits best?
options: Paper copies prepared in large print and braille
A one-to-one interview with the items read aloud
A web form that players fill in on their phones
A group talk about nerves before competition
rationales: Alternative print formats give privacy to those who read them. Some players use neither format, so they would again need to answer to somebody.
Reading items aloud is a fair accommodation for a player who wants it. Having to voice answers to staff is what these players objected to.
Each player already has a phone set up to suit their own vision, so a properly built form lets all of them answer independently and in private, as sighted athletes do.
A group talk can bring out shared experience. It would not yield individual ratings, and it makes answers more public than last year's survey did.
takeaway: Accessible assessment means equal privacy and independence, not just access to the items.

stem: Idris, a collegiate 10,000-meter runner, is sent to a consultant during Ramadan. His coach writes that he is "flat, probably the fasting." Idris says he has fasted through five track seasons and runs after the evening meal on a plan made with the dietitian. His training log shows steady workout times in those earlier seasons. This year they began to slip in late January, the week the coach split the distance runners into two squads, and Ramadan started a month later. What should the consultant explore next?
options: How he is eating and sleeping during the fast
What keeping the fast means to him this year
How his coach responds to him while he is fasting
What the new training squads have been like for him
rationales: Fueling and sleep would come first if the slump had begun with the fast. It began a month earlier, and the same routine has worked for five seasons.
Asking about meaning is worthwhile if he seems torn or alone in his practice. He describes a settled practice, and the timing points elsewhere.
Strained support would matter if trouble tracked the coach's reactions to fasting. The slip was under way before there was any fasting to react to.

The log ties the start of the slip to the squad change rather than to the fast. Culturally responsive assessment tests a referral source's cultural explanation against the data instead of adopting it.
takeaway: Treat a cultural explanation as a hypothesis and check it against the timeline.

topic: Locating the strain in a transition
stem: Terrence, a first-year rugby player at a university far from home, has missed four early lifts. He has won a starting place and calls the rugby "easier than I thought." His grades are good, and he works the same warehouse hours he worked through high school. Asked about the lifts, he says, "Back home my uncle had the kettle on and Dre was outside with the car. I've been up before six since I was twelve. Here the alarm goes and there's nobody." In Wylleman and Lavallee's developmental model, at which level is his transition strain?
options: At the athletic level
At the psychological level
At the psychosocial level
At the academic–vocational level
rationales: Strain at this level comes from the step up in training and competition. He is starting and finds the rugby manageable.
This level concerns developmental tasks such as forming an identity in late adolescence. He describes missing companions rather than uncertainty about who he is.
The habit of early rising always ran on people: an uncle, a friend with a car. What the move changed is the set of relationships around his sport, which is the model's psychosocial level.
Study and work fall at this level and can crowd out training. His grades are sound and his work hours have not changed.
takeaway: The developmental model asks which of several simultaneous transitions is carrying the strain.

stem: In a first meeting, Dashiell, a professional contemporary dancer, says he is gay and asks whether the consultant has worked with LGBTQ+ performers. "A few," she says. "I'm still learning, and I'd want you to tell me if I miss something." He leans back. "That's more than the last two admitted. One of them kept me on coming out for a month. I'd come about casting calls." He says he would like to go ahead with her, and casting anxiety is an area she knows well. What should she do next?
options: Begin on what happens to him at casting calls
Ask what being understood would look like to him
Offer names of colleagues with more such experience
Describe what her LGBTQ+ clients have taught her
rationales: He has asked about her experience, had a candid answer, and chosen to go on. His complaint about earlier providers is that they made his identity the topic, so responsiveness here means turning to his concern.
This question suits a client who says that past providers failed to understand his life. His story is of providers who would not leave the subject.
Other names help a client who wants someone with closer knowledge. He has heard the limits of hers and wants to continue, and his concern is one she is competent to address.
Saying more could help if he doubted her answer. He was satisfied with it, and more talk would put off his reason for coming.
takeaway: Cultural responsiveness sometimes means answering the question honestly and then getting to work on the client's concern.

stem: On the first morning of a camp, a consultant interviewed each member of a visiting national field hockey team through the team's own interpreter. Answers were a few words long, and eyes stayed lowered. Her draft says "low confidence, weak communication." Over the next three days she hears the same players shouting corrections across the pitch and disputing calls with the umpire. At breakfast, two of them tell their physio at length how well they are striking the ball, the same interpreter beside them. Which reading of the interviews fits these data best?
options: The players were short of confidence
The players were reserved with a stranger
The players were deferring to seniority
The players were misunderstanding the questions
rationales: Low confidence should appear in more than one place. The players correct one another, dispute calls, and speak well of their own form.
The quiet appears with an unfamiliar interviewer and disappears with teammates, an umpire, and a physio they know. It says something about the interview rather than about confidence or communication.
Deference would show as looking to, or waiting for, senior members. The interviews were one at a time, and players openly corrected each other.
A language problem would be likely if the interpreting were poor. With the same interpreter they talk freely.
takeaway: Before labeling a trait, check whether the behavior follows the person or the setting.

stem: A consultant's intake form asks for "mother's name," "father's name," and gender, each with fixed blanks or boxes. Maren, a 24-year-old climber, says the page made her feel she had to account for herself before she had sat down. Going back through two years of files, the consultant sees that she never drew on those answers. What she used came from the first conversation, when she asks every client how they would like to be addressed and who they turn to for support. What should she do about these items?
options: Add a wider set of boxes to each of them
Take both of them off the form
Replace the boxes with open blanks
Mark both of them as optional
rationales: More categories help when answers must be counted in a standard way. Nothing is being counted here, and boxes still ask clients to fit themselves in.
The answers have served no purpose, and what she does need is already gathered from every client in conversation. Intake should ask for information that is relevant to the service.
Open blanks suit information that is used but poorly captured by set categories. This information goes unused, so clients would still be explaining themselves for nothing.
Optional items make sense when the form itself cannot be changed. It is her own form, and skipping an item can still feel like a statement.
takeaway: Ask at intake for what the work will use; an unused identity question costs the client something.

topic: Framing goals around a client's values
stem: Maeve, a collegiate softball pitcher, is setting goals for the spring. Last year's strikeout goal "felt like homework." The team's goal of reaching the conference final moved her, but by April, she says, "I couldn't have told you if I'd had a hand in it." Asked for her best day, she picks a game with no strikeouts, after which the shortstop hugged her and said, "You kept us busy all night." She wants something to work on each time she pitches. Which goal fits best?
options: "Keep my changeup at the knees in bullpen sessions."
"Help us hold opponents to three runs a game."
"Help us get back to the conference final."
"Throw early strikes so my infield gets to play."
rationales: This is a controllable process goal and would suit someone driven by her own craft. Nothing in it touches the teammates who made her best day her best.
A team performance goal ties her to others, but nine players produce the number. She would be back to wondering what her part had been.
The shared outcome stirred her last year and gave her nothing to judge her own part by.
Early strikes are hers to work on every time she pitches, and the goal is framed by what matters to her: giving teammates a part in the game.
takeaway: Controllable goals hold better when framed by what the client values, including contribution to others.

stem: A community soccer league wants a consultant to help parents of its 10- to 13-year-olds handle the ride home after games, when, players say, "the replay starts." Interviews show that most parents work evenings and weekends and ride shared vans or buses to games. Practices have just been cut to 50 minutes, and parents rarely attend them. When a field changes, the team managers post it in group chats, with English, Spanish, and Vietnamese versions, and nearly every household replies within the hour. Which delivery plan fits best?
options: A weekend workshop with interpreters on hand
Short clips posted to the team group chats
Brief segments built into team practices
Printed handouts sent home with the players
rationales: Interpreters remove one barrier to a workshop. With parents at work on evenings and weekends and dependent on shared transport, few could be there.
The plan has to reach parents, and the chats already do, in the languages they use and on their own schedule. It builds on a working resource instead of fighting time and transport.
Practice segments reach players and coaches without extra travel. The aim is a change in parents, who are rarely there, and practice time has just shrunk.
Handouts help where phones or data are scarce. These households answer messages within the hour, and paper relies on players to pass it on.
takeaway: Plan delivery around channels a community already uses.

stem: Ignacio, 31, a national-team kayaker, will retire after the world championships in 18 months. His program asks consultants to begin transition goals at that point. Ignacio has a job waiting at the boat workshop where he has spent four off-seasons, coaches his daughter's robotics team, and grins when asked about life after racing. He is healthy and has made every team for six years. Then he shows the consultant video of two finals he lost in the first 50 meters: "That's what wakes me up at night." What should the plan center on?
options: His composure and reactions at the start
His interests and roles outside of racing
His meetings with a career advisor
His coping with an earlier end to racing
rationales: Vocation, roles outside sport, and expectations for retirement are already in place, so transition goals would be planned for the program's sake. His own concern and the performance data point to the start.
Broadening an exclusive athletic identity is important before retirement. Ignacio already has a trade, a parenting role, and things he looks forward to.
Career advising helps an athlete who needs a vocational direction. His job is arranged and he knows it well.
Preparing for an unplanned exit suits an athlete whose place or health is in doubt. Ignacio is healthy and has been selected without a break.
takeaway: Transition theory informs the plan; the client's actual readiness decides how much of it is needed.

topic: Responding to a microaggression in a workshop
stem: In a workshop with a collegiate women's basketball team, one player asks a teammate of Korean descent, "But where are you really from?" The room goes quiet. "Toledo, like I put on the roster," the teammate says. "You can do better than that one." The player reddens: "You're right. That was lazy, I'm sorry." The teammate nods, others murmur agreement, and the two go back to arguing happily over the next drill. It is the first such remark the consultant has heard in this group. What should the consultant do?
options: Name the remark's impact, and restate the group's norms
Pause the activity, and open up a group discussion
Carry on with the activity, and check on the teammate later
Carry on with the activity, and talk to the asker later
rationales: The facilitator should speak when the target is left to carry the moment alone. She has named the remark herself, and the player took it in; repeating it would take the moment away from her.
A discussion fits when remarks like this are a pattern the group has not faced. This was a first instance, and the players have settled it.

The target spoke for herself, the player apologized without defending it, and the group backed her. A private check-in later allows for any impact that didn't show without reopening the matter in public.
A private talk with the asker suits someone who misses the point or keeps doing it. She saw the problem at once and apologized.
takeaway: Facilitators make sure impact is acknowledged; when the group has done so, a private check-in may be enough.

stem: Two police recruits stay behind before the first class of a breath-focused stress program. "Somebody at our church said these classes have you chanting to something," one says. "We don't do that." The other adds, "If it's just breathing, fine. Nobody's told us what it is." The course, which the academy requires, involves paced breathing and noticing when attention wanders, with no chanting or devotional content. How should the consultant respond?
options: Teach them an attention exercise that uses no breathing
Put them in touch with the academy chaplain to talk it over
Ask the academy to make the course optional for recruits
Tell them what the classes do and don't include
rationales: An alternative with the same aim is right for recruits whose objection stands once they know what the practice is. These two object to something the course doesn't contain.
A chaplain can help recruits who want religious guidance on a practice. They have not asked for guidance; they lack information that the consultant has.
Seeking a change in the requirement makes sense if an informed objection can't be accommodated. There is no informed objection yet.
Their concern rests on a rumor about content, and one says plainly what would make it fine. An accurate description respects their faith and lets them judge for themselves.
takeaway: Find out whether a values concern is about the practice itself or about what someone has heard of it.

topic: Adjusting imagery for a blind athlete
stem: Thandeka, an elite para judoka who has been blind since birth, has rebuilt her imagery script with her consultant around grips, footfalls, and the shift of her opponent's weight. She practices it on the mat in her judogi. "It's all in there," she reports, "and the throw comes off in the time it really takes. But I could be folding laundry. Then Saturday comes and my mouth is dry and my heart's going, and it's like I've never been there before." What should they change next?
options: Add more touch and sound to the throws
Add the nerves and urgency of a match
Rehearse the throws at true match speed
Rehearse on the mat, dressed for a match
rationales: Richer tactile and auditory detail would help if the script seemed thin or relied on sight. She says the content is all there.
The script has the task, setting, and timing but none of the feelings of competition, so match day feels new. PETTLEP's emotion element calls for imaging the emotions and arousal of the real event.
Matching real timing is another PETTLEP element. Her throws already take the time they really take.
Physical and environmental similarity support functional equivalence. She already practices on the mat in her judogi.
takeaway: PETTLEP is a checklist: find the element that is missing for this athlete.

stem: At season's end, a consultant to a professional women's soccer team reads unsigned evaluation forms, completed in players' own languages and collected by the players' union. Ratings average 9 of 10, with little spread. The comments are just as warm, and nearly every form also objects to something: the Monday slot, a role-play that dragged, the slides. A coach waves the numbers away: "Half of them come from clubs where you'd never criticize staff." How should the consultant treat the ratings?
options: Report the ratings as credible evidence
Report the ratings as inflated by politeness
Report the ratings separately by players' origin
Hold the ratings, and repeat the form in midseason
rationales: The forms were unsigned, independent, and in players' own languages, and the same players criticized freely. The coach's claim about their background predicts something the data don't show.
Politeness could inflate signed forms handed to the consultant. These were unsigned and independently collected, and players criticized specifics freely.
Separate reporting would be useful if ratings differed by group. They have little spread, and splitting them would build the coach's assumption into the report.
Repeating a form helps when it was given before players knew the program well. It was given at the end of the season.
takeaway: Cultural knowledge suggests a threat to validity; the data decide whether it is there.

stem: A club consultant has worked for a season with Jonas, a 27-year-old hockey forward whose contract will not be renewed. Her role with him ends in two weeks, and he has booked both remaining sessions. He is sad but sleeping well and seeing friends, and a players' association advisor starts with him on the first of the month. "We'll do a proper goodbye in the last one," he says. A club overseas has invited him to a three-day tryout on Tuesday. "I know hockey's been my whole self," he says. "The advisor and I start on that." What should the first remaining session focus on?
options: Who he is and could be outside of hockey
What support he can draw on after the club
What he needs mentally for the tryout
What he has gained over the past season
rationales: Exploring identity is valuable after deselection, and he agrees. He has help arranged for it, with time to do it, and the tryout is days away.
Connecting a client with continuing support is a key part of concluding. An advisor is already in place and friends are close.
Support and a closing session are already arranged, and he is coping. The time-limited need, and the one he raises, is readying himself for Tuesday.
Reviewing gains belongs in a closing session, which he has already placed in the last meeting.
takeaway: Concluding well means using the remaining time for what isn't already covered.

topic: Revising a plan for acculturation stress
stem: Seo-yeon, a first-year collegiate golfer who moved from overseas for school, is six weeks into work on her pre-shot routine. Video shows the routine complete on nearly all shots, in practice and in tournaments alike. Her classes are going well. Her scores at home events match her practice rounds, but on road trips they climb after the first day. Her journal for those weekends reads: "Ate in my room. Thought up a joke in English, and they'd moved on. Didn't sleep much." Which change to the plan fits these data best?
options: Add crowd and scoring pressure to routine practice
Arrange support for her coursework in English
Shorten the routine to spare effort late in rounds
Add goals for connecting with teammates on trips
rationales: Simulated pressure helps a routine that breaks down in competition. Hers holds in tournaments, and her home scores show it.
Academic language support would fit if study demands were wearing her down. Her classes are going well.
A shorter routine suits a player whose steps fall away as she tires. The routine is complete on nearly all shots.
The routine is intact, and scores slip where she is isolated and losing sleep. Reassessment points to acculturation stress on road trips, so the plan should grow to address connection there.
takeaway: When a skill is intact and scores still vary, look at the context in which they vary.

stem: A consultant leads mental skills for a running program for adults resettled after fleeing conflict. On feedback forms, runners say she asks rather than assumes, owns her mistakes, and reworks exercises that don't suit them. One writes, "I'm glad you ask me. But you are the fourth one to ask, and I am tired of explaining what an asylum hearing is." Two others say much the same. Which next step in her development best fits this feedback?
options: Keep a journal of the assumptions she brings
Study the circumstances that her clients live with
Practice adapting techniques with a supervisor
Invite clients to say more about their backgrounds
rationales: Self-reflection builds awareness of her own assumptions, one of the multicultural competencies. Runners already see her questioning them.

Her awareness and flexibility are evident. What is missing is knowledge of clients' worlds, and leaving clients to supply it has become a burden. Multicultural competence includes learning on one's own time.
Supervised practice builds culturally appropriate skills. Runners say she already reworks exercises that don't suit them.
Asking clients reflects cultural humility, and she does it well. More asking would add to the load they describe.
takeaway: Humility means asking about the person; competence includes not making clients teach you what you could look up.

stem: Reviewing two years of case notes, a consultant sees that Dante, a 19-year-old boxer, is "not really committed." He had moved three sessions because his delivery shifts changed, and had made up each one. She had used the phrase for two other athletes, both of whom moved sessions for work. Athletes who moved as many for exams or family trips are "busy" or "juggling a lot." She recalls her own college years, when her parents paid her way. She enjoys Dante and leaves sessions with him energized. What does her phrase most likely reflect?
options: A standard set by an advantaged upbringing
A reaction carried over from a past relationship
A sign that her caseload is wearing her out
A fair reading of his readiness to change
rationales: The same behavior earns a different label depending on whether a paid job caused it, and paid work is what she never had to fit around sport. Seeing how one's social position shapes judgment is the work of self-reflexivity.
Countertransference would show as feelings tied to a particular person from her past. The phrase spans several athletes, and she enjoys Dante.
Strain would show across clients and in her energy. Her sessions with Dante leave her energized, and the label follows one kind of reason.
The phrase would be fair if Dante were avoiding the work. He has made up each session.
takeaway: Compare how you label the same behavior in different clients; the pattern may be about you.

topic: Competence and choice for a Deaf client
stem: Nerys, a collegiate wrestler who is Deaf and uses American Sign Language, asks the athletic department's consultant for help with pre-match nerves. The consultant doesn't sign and has not worked with Deaf athletes; a colleague on the same staff signs fluently and has openings. The consultant lays out several ways they could work. Nerys says she has no tie to either of them, adding, "In the training room it's me, the trainer, and an interpreter. Same with my professors. I'd love one conversation with just two people in it, in my language." What should the consultant do?
options: Arrange a qualified interpreter, and seek consultation
Hold sessions by typed chat, and review how it goes
Invite the colleague to co-lead, and learn from her
Refer Nerys to the colleague, and help with the handoff
rationales: An interpreter plus consultation is a sound way to extend competence when a client chooses this consultant or no signing provider exists. Nerys wants a conversation without a third person, and a signing colleague is free.
Typed chat leaves two people in the conversation and suits a client who prefers it. English on a screen is not the language Nerys asks for.
Co-leading helps a client who wants to stay with a consultant still building competence. It would put a third person back in the room.
The colleague alone can offer what Nerys describes: direct conversation in ASL between two people, with fitting competence. She has no tie to this consultant that would weigh against it.
takeaway: Extending competence is one ethical path; a better-placed colleague the client would prefer is another.

stem: A consultant with a collegiate football program hears the linebackers coach call an injured player "soft" and praise another for "never bothering the trainers." The other position coaches talk about injuries matter-of-factly, as the head coach has asked them to. The athletic trainer's figures show steady early reports of minor injuries from every position group except the linebackers, whose reports have stopped. After practice the linebackers coach, who respects the consultant, asks, "You've been watching me. What am I doing that I can't see?" Which step should the consultant take first?
options: Raise the program's injury culture with leadership
Lead a session with all players on reporting injuries
Tell the coach how his remarks may affect reporting
Urge the linebackers to get injuries checked early
rationales: Going to leadership fits a pattern that runs through the staff. Here leadership has set the tone and one coach departs from it, and he has just asked for feedback.
A team session fits if players in general keep injuries to themselves. Every other group reports early, so the players' general attitude is not the problem.

The figures place the problem with one group and one coach's remarks, and he has opened the door. Direct, respectful feedback to the person who can change it is the smallest step that addresses the risk.
Encouraging players to seek evaluation is right whenever one is known to be hurt. It leaves in place the remarks that make reporting costly, and no particular injury has come to light.
takeaway: Let the pattern show where a culture problem sits, and intervene at that level.

stem: On a video call, a consultant told Emilio, a professional esports player born and raised in Texas, "Your English is really good." At the next session Emilio said that people often assume he isn't American. The consultant acknowledged having made that assumption and apologized without explaining it away. "Appreciate it. Most people get weird," Emilio said. Two sessions on, he is as frank as ever, and he has sent a clip of a scrim he "choked" for today. The consultant still loses sleep over the remark. How should the consultant open today's session?
options: Apologize again, naming the assumption it carried
Turn to the scrim clip that he sent for today
Ask how the remark has affected their work together
Ask if he would rather work with another consultant
rationales: A fuller apology would be due if the first one had been vague or defensive. It named the assumption, and Emilio accepted it; repeating it asks him to tend to the consultant's guilt.

The impact was acknowledged, Emilio accepted the apology, and his openness suggests the repair has held. What remains is the consultant's own distress, which belongs in supervision rather than in his session.
Checking on the alliance suits signs of lingering strain. Emilio is frank and is bringing hard material.
Offering a change respects a client who doubts that he can go on. He has shown no such doubt.
takeaway: After a repair is accepted, don't make the client look after your guilt.

stem: Harper, a newly certified consultant, has spent six weeks with a professional baseball organization and has an idea for between-pitch routines. Her notes on staff meetings record that two suggestions from newer staff met silence. One came back a week later from the hitting coach, to nods all around. An analyst who arrived when she did "gets everything through"; Harper has seen him in the hitting coach's office most Friday afternoons. Papers from the general manager's office are read out and not mentioned again. What should she do with her idea?
options: Talk it over with the hitting coach first
Present it at the next staff meeting
Put it in writing to the general manager
Try it out with a few interested players
rationales: Her notes show that ideas are taken up when the hitting coach carries them and stall when newer staff or the front office put them forward. Acting on unwritten rules like this one is contextual intelligence.
Presenting openly suits a staff that takes up ideas from whoever raises them. Newer staff who tried it met silence.
A paper to the general manager would fit if decisions came from that office. Its papers are read out and dropped.
A small trial suits a staff that is won over by seeing results. Nothing in her notes suggests that ideas travel up from players.
takeaway: Contextual intelligence means reading how things get done here before choosing how to act.

topic: Scope in responding to a bias incident
stem: A technology company retains a consultant for leadership and team communication. After an employee complains that a manager mimicked his accent in a meeting, an executive calls: "You know that team, and everyone trusts you. Could you talk to the two of them and to whoever was in the room, find out what was said, and tell me whether it crosses the line? We'd act on whatever you conclude." The company has a human resources department, which has not yet been told. What should the consultant do?
options: Lead a conversation between the two of them
Direct the executive to human resources
Lead a workshop with the team on its communication
Recommend a specialist in inclusion to train the staff
rationales: A facilitated conversation can help repair a working relationship when both want it and any complaint has been resolved. This complaint hasn't been looked into, and the executive wants a finding.

The executive is asking for an investigation and a judgment on alleged discriminatory conduct. That is the organization's formal process, and taking it on would conflict with the consultant's trusted role with the team.
A communication workshop is within the consultant's role. It would not answer an unexamined complaint and could seem to spread the responsibility around.
Specialist-led training fits a wish to build inclusion across the company. The request concerns what happened in one meeting.
takeaway: Trust with a team doesn't make a consultant its investigator.

stem: Liv, an elite alpine skier, is nine weeks past ACL reconstruction. For six weeks she completed 95% of her rehab sessions; since then, about half. "It's the same knee, only better built," she said at week three, and she says it still. Her mood ratings have stayed steady and high. She rehabbed back from two earlier injuries without missing a day. In week seven her rehab moved to a clinic across the city, where she sees a different therapist each visit, at hours that overlap her team's video meetings. Using the integrated model of response to sport injury, which part should the plan address first?
options: How she appraises the injury and her recovery
How she responds emotionally to the injury
Personal factors she brought to the injury
Situational factors surrounding her rehab
rationales: Appraisal drives emotion and behavior in the model and is often the target. Hers is realistic, hopeful, and unchanged across the drop in adherence.
Emotional response would be the target if low mood were eroding adherence. Her mood has stayed steady and high.
Injury history, personality, and coping skills are personal factors. Hers carried her through two earlier injuries and the first six weeks of this one.
Adherence fell when the setting changed: a distant clinic, rotating therapists, and clashing hours. In the integrated model these are situational factors that shape behavioral responses.
takeaway: In the integrated model, find what changed when the behavior changed.

stem: A ballet company asks a consultant to help reduce injuries during its audition season. In interviews, dancers call auditions "the fun part" and expect to do well. They lean on one another, and it has been a settled year for most of them. Accident reports have a theme: "Didn't see her coming from the side." "My shoulders were up by my ears and I landed stiff." Based on the stress–injury model, which component should the prevention program start with?
options: Relaxation and attention-control training
Restructuring of audition-related thoughts
Team building to widen social support
Help with moves and other life changes
rationales: The reports describe the stress response itself, muscle tension and narrowed peripheral vision. The model's interventions target that physiological and attentional side as well as appraisal, and appraisal is favorable here.
Changing appraisals is the model's other intervention target. These dancers see auditions as enjoyable and expect to do well.
Social support is a coping resource in the model, and building it helps isolated dancers. These dancers already rely on one another.
A history of stressors raises vulnerability in the model. It has been a settled year for most of the dancers.
takeaway: Match injury-prevention work to the part of the stress–injury model that the data point to.

stem: Curtis, a firefighter, is eight weeks past shoulder surgery. His exercise log shows each prescribed set ticked, then a column he has added himself: ten more, twenty more, a run of push-ups. "The guys are covering my shifts," he says. "I'm not going to sit around." His physical therapist reports that the joint is irritated most Mondays and that his progress has stalled. With Curtis's consent, she and the consultant are planning goals with him. Which goal fits best?
options: "Complete my prescribed sets, and tick each one off."
"Stop at my prescribed sets, and log my rest days."
"Gain a set number of degrees of motion each week."
"Return to my engine on a date we fix together."
rationales: A completion goal helps someone who skips exercises. Curtis already ticks off every set; the trouble starts after that.
The log and the Monday irritation point to over-adherence. A process goal that counts stopping and resting as success turns his drive toward what recovery needs.
A weekly target makes progress visible when rehab seems endless. For someone already overdoing it, a number to beat would feed the problem.
A date can sustain someone who has lost sight of the purpose. Curtis has purpose in plenty, and a deadline would add to his hurry.
takeaway: Over-adherence is an adherence problem too; goals can reward restraint.

stem: Odessa, a collegiate lacrosse player, is rehabbing a dislocated shoulder. Her log shows every set done except the last two, small rotations with a light band. "Those are the warm-up ones for old people, right?" she says. "I do the ones that make me strong." She feels good about her progress, finds the band work easy, and is happy for the consultant to speak with her athletic trainer about this. Which step should the consultant take first?
options: Teach Odessa self-talk for the final sets
Set completion goals for the final sets
Ask the trainer to explain the final sets to her
Ask the trainer to alter the final sets for her
rationales: Self-talk can help an athlete who doubts she can finish or gives up from fatigue. Odessa finds these sets easy and leaves them out on purpose.
Goals and tracking help an athlete who means to finish and loses track. Odessa is leaving out sets she sees no use in.
She skips the sets because she misjudges what they are for. Explaining an exercise's purpose is the athletic trainer's role, and Odessa has agreed to the contact.
Altering exercises is the trainer's call and worth raising if she can't do them safely or comfortably. She finds them easy.
takeaway: Find the reason behind a skipped exercise, and go to the professional whose role covers it.

stem: Rosalba, a 58-year-old triathlete, is recovering from knee surgery. Twice a day she wears a brace that holds a gentle stretch for half an hour; it sets itself, and she has nothing to do but sit. Her physical therapist has told her to expect a dull, harmless ache. "My leg's loose and I'm breathing fine," she tells the consultant. "I just sit there staring at my knee, and after ten minutes the ache is the only thing in the world." Which strategy should the consultant suggest for these half hours?
options: Get absorbed in a story or music
Follow the sensations in her knee closely
Breathe slowly and let the leg go loose
Take the brace off and call the therapist
rationales: The ache is expected and harmless, the task asks nothing of her attention, and dwelling on the ache magnifies it. Dissociative strategies suit exactly that kind of pain.
Associative attention helps when sensations must guide effort or form. The brace does the work, and watching the knee is what makes the ache grow.
Paced breathing and muscle release suit someone who braces against pain. Her leg is loose and her breathing easy.
Stopping and contacting the therapist is right for new or sharp pain. This is the ache the therapist described.
takeaway: Choose a pain strategy by what the pain signals and what the task needs from attention.

stem: In a session at school before hockey practice, Ronan, 16, mentions that since a hard hit two days ago he has had headaches, can't concentrate in class, and wears sunglasses indoors. He is alert, walks steadily, and says it is no worse than yesterday. He has told no one, because Friday is a playoff game, and asks the consultant to keep it between them. The athletic trainer is in the training room down the hall, getting ready for practice. What should the consultant do first?
options: Call emergency services, and stay with him until they arrive
Phone his parents, and ask them to arrange a medical visit
Continue the session, within the limits he has been given
Walk him to the athletic trainer, and explain why on the way
rationales: Emergency care is right for red flags such as worsening headache, repeated vomiting, or growing drowsiness. He is alert and steady, and his symptoms are not worsening.
His parents need to know, and they would be the route if no medical staff were at hand. With the athletic trainer down the hall and practice about to start, this is slower.
Mental skills work can go on alongside medical management. No one has evaluated him, so there are no limits to work within.
A suspected concussion in a minor needs medical evaluation before any further play, and confidentiality does not extend to withholding this risk. The professional responsible is steps away.
takeaway: Suspected concussion goes to the medical team the same day, whatever the game schedule.

stem: Brigid, a collegiate volleyball setter, is three months into rehab for a torn Achilles tendon. She eats with the team, travels to matches, and charts opponents' serves. Her roommate hears about the bad days. Her therapist has walked her through each stage. She has missed four of her last ten rehab visits; the clinic is two buses away, and on crutches, she says, "it eats the whole afternoon." She would be glad for the consultant to talk with her coach. Which strategy should the consultant suggest?
options: Give her a part in team meetings
Help arrange rides to her clinic
Set aside time to hear how she is
Go over what her return will involve
rationales: A team role supports belonging for an injured athlete who feels cut off. She is with the team at meals and matches and already has a job to do.
Belonging, emotional, and informational support are all in place. What keeps her from rehab is the journey, so tangible support is the kind that is missing.
Emotional support helps an athlete who has nobody to talk to. Her roommate fills that role.
Informational support eases uncertainty. Her therapist has explained each stage.
takeaway: Social support works when its type fits the need.

stem: Yuna, an elite figure skater, has six weeks left in a boot after an ankle fracture. Her surgeon is pleased with the bone, she has had no pain for weeks, and she hasn't missed an exercise. She keeps pulling up old videos of her triple Lutz. "I used to know the edge without thinking," she tells her consultant. "Last night I tried to feel the takeoff and it was blurry." Her physical therapist has no objection to imagery work. Which imagery should the consultant introduce?
options: Imagery of the bone knitting together
Imagery of soothing warmth in the ankle
Imagery of her jump takeoffs and edges
Imagery of working through her exercises
rationales: Healing imagery can give an athlete a sense of involvement in recovery. Healing is going well and isn't on her mind.
Pain-management imagery suits discomfort during rehab. She has had no pain for weeks.
Her concern is losing the feel of a skill she can't practice. Rehearsal imagery keeps the skill mentally active while the ankle heals.
Imaging rehab tasks supports motivation and adherence. She hasn't missed an exercise.
takeaway: In rehab, imagery can serve healing, pain, adherence, or skill; choose by the athlete's need.

stem: Femi, a professional soccer midfielder, was medically cleared nine months after ACL reconstruction and has spent five weeks in full-contact training. Since clearance his readiness scores have risen from 48 to 91 of 100. The performance analyst's video shows him tackling and cutting at his pre-injury rates. "Yesterday I had to think which knee it was," he laughs. His head coach, whose last player back from this injury "came apart in a month," urges more sessions, twice a week. What should the consultant propose to Femi?
options: Confirm that his goals are met, and space out the sessions
Add confidence work that is built around contact
Return to the medical team before any further sessions
Keep the present plan, and repeat the scale in a month
rationales: Scores, video, and his own account agree that he is confident and playing freely. The coach's worry comes from another player, and the evidence supports tapering the work.
More confidence work is needed when clearance outpaces readiness. Femi's scores and his tackling show that the two have come together.
New physical signs call for the medical team. None are reported, and they have cleared him.
Waiting is sensible while readiness is still developing or hasn't been tested by contact. He has had five weeks of contact with clear gains.
takeaway: Clearance and readiness can differ; when they converge, let the plan wind down.

topic: Recognizing a clinical concern in rehab
stem: At a progress review three months into rehab for a back injury, Carmen, a collegiate gymnast, says rehab itself is on schedule. For the past several weeks, though, she has felt hopeless nearly every day, sleeps badly, and has stopped answering friends and going to class. "I can't see the point anymore." Asked directly, she says she has had no thoughts of suicide or of harming herself and has no plan. She isn't seeing anyone else for support. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Adjust her rehab goals, and keep an eye on her mood
Follow the crisis plan, and stay with her until help comes
Ask her consent to coordinate with her current therapist
Help her connect with a licensed mental health provider
rationales: Setbacks often bring brief dips in mood that goals and support can help. Weeks of near-daily hopelessness, withdrawal, and poor sleep while rehab goes well are beyond that.
The crisis plan is for imminent risk. Asked directly, she reports no suicidal thoughts and no plan, so this is urgent to refer but not an emergency.
Coordinating is right when a client already has licensed care. She isn't seeing anyone.
Persistent hopelessness, sleep problems, and withdrawal need evaluation by a licensed professional, which is outside a CMPC's scope. With no imminent risk, the step is a prompt, supported referral.
takeaway: Persistent, wide-ranging low mood calls for referral; imminent risk calls for the emergency plan.

stem: Rodrigo, an elite wheelchair basketball player, had met every weekly goal since shoulder surgery. He arrives for his progress review straight from his surgeon's office. A complication has added eight weeks, and he will miss the world championships. He understands the new protocol and starts it Thursday. When the consultant takes out the goal sheet, he pushes it back across the table, jaw tight. "I've been counting down to that tournament for two years," he says, and stares out of the window. What should the consultant do now?
options: Reset his weekly goals to the surgeon's timeline
Hear what losing the tournament means to him
Go over the gains he has made since surgery
Help him list questions to take back to the surgeon
rationales: New short-term goals will be needed, and in a few days they will probably help. He has just had the news and has pushed the sheet away.
The loss is minutes old and large. Attending to his emotional response comes before planning, which can wait until he is ready and the new protocol begins.
Reviewing gains helps someone who believes that nothing has been achieved. He is grieving a tournament, and progress charts would speak past that.
Preparing questions helps a client who is unsure what the news involves. He understands the protocol.
takeaway: After a fresh setback, the emotional response comes first and the goal revision follows.

stem: Rin, a professional esports player with chronic wrist pain, was offered surgery or a longer course of conservative treatment. On a video call she tells her consultant, "I'm having the surgery. I asked two surgeons everything on my list, and I've slept on it." The consultant would have expected her to wait until after a tournament in the spring. Rin goes on, "My manager's going to go quiet on me. I've written the message four times and deleted it." What is the most appropriate response?
options: Help her think through which option matters more to her
Help her draw up questions about the two treatments
Help her prepare to tell her manager what she decided
Help her set up another medical opinion on her wrist
rationales: Clarifying priorities is useful, and within scope, for a client who is torn. Rin has decided; reopening the choice would reflect the consultant's doubts rather than her need.
Preparing questions supports a client who lacks information. She has put hers to two surgeons.
The treatment choice belongs to Rin and her medical team, and it is made. Her difficulty is the conversation ahead, which is squarely within mental performance work.
Encouraging another opinion is reasonable when a client doubts the advice she was given. She has had two and is settled.
takeaway: Medical choices belong to the client and the medical team; help with what the client is facing around them.

stem: Yusra, an injured collegiate soccer player, signed a release letting her consultant share her attendance and mental skills plan with the sports medicine staff. At the staff's weekly meeting, the physical therapist turns to the consultant: "How's Yusra's plan going? Is she showing up?" Around the table are two athletic trainers, the team physician, and, as of this month, an assistant coach and an academic adviser who sit in to hear about availability. How should the consultant handle the request at this meeting?
options: Share nothing about Yusra's sessions
Share her attendance and her plan
Share her attendance, not her plan
Share her attendance, plan, and concerns
rationales: The release covers the sports medicine staff, and two people now at the table are outside it. The consultant can give the authorized information to the staff separately.
This is what the release allows, to the people it names. The coach and the adviser are not among them.
A limited disclosure needs a release that covers it for everyone present. Attendance is as protected from the coach and adviser as the plan is.
Concerns could be shared with the medical staff if Yusra had agreed to it. Her release doesn't mention them, and others are present.
takeaway: A release specifies both what may be shared and with whom; check who is in the room.

stem: An athletic trainer asks a consultant about Corbin, a wrestler three weeks into recovery from a broken forearm. He was miserable the Saturday he missed a meet and back to joking by Monday. He comes to rehab, does his work, and can recite his timeline, including the two meets still to miss. He sleeps fine and eats with the team. "He never got angry," the trainer says. "I was taught that they go through stages, and I keep waiting for the rest." Based on research on responses to sport injury, what should the consultant suggest?
options: Help Corbin voice anger that he might be holding in
Help Corbin see a licensed mental health provider
Carry on with his rehab and her usual check-ins
Go over his recovery timeline with him once more
rationales: Making room for anger helps when there are signs of it. There are none, and research doesn't support a set sequence that an athlete must complete.
A referral fits persistent distress or changes in sleep, eating, or functioning. He had one hard day and is doing well.
Fixed stage models are poorly supported; responses vary with appraisal and circumstances. Corbin's appraisal is realistic and he is adherent, so nothing more is called for.
Reviewing the timeline helps when cheerfulness rests on a misunderstanding. He can recite his, with the meets he will miss.
takeaway: Athletes don't have to pass through set stages; watch how this one appraises and copes.
